RAMQ – Naître sans filet social: RAMQ – Born Without a Safety Net
Nous ne pouvions pas payer, donc nous so: “We couldn’t pay, so we went home without a doctor seeing my daughter.”
La fille de Ridwan et de Durowoju Sulaim: Ridwan and Durowoju Sulaimon’s daughter was born on February 4 at the Hôpital du Sacré-Cœur-de-Montréal. Like all the little Quebecers born that day, she received Canadian citizenship. Her parents, both temporary residence permit holders from Nigeria, believed this entitled her to health care paid for by the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ). They would soon discover it didn’t. Children born in Quebec to parents holding a temporary work or study permit, or who are undocumented, are not eligible for RAMQ. When these children need health care, their parents must pay for it out of pocket. The bill sometimes runs to tens of thousands of dollars, with serious consequences for families.
Dans le cas des Sulaimon, non seulement: In the Sulaimons’ case, not only was the baby ineligible for RAMQ, but because of a misunderstanding, mother and child had no access to private insurance either. That misunderstanding cost the family more than $20,000. “When I came to study at Concordia, I thought my family would have access to the university’s insurance, just like me,” says Ridwan Sulaimon, the baby’s father.
Or, ils ont changé leur politique, de so: “But they changed their policy, so their insurance no longer covers dependants. They say they tried to warn us by email, but I never received anything. If I had known, I wouldn’t have come with my family.” The Sulaimons only understood the seriousness of their situation after their daughter was born.
Sachant que la facture ne cessait d’augm: Knowing the bill kept growing, they left the hospital the day after their child’s birth. They still received three bills totalling about $9,000. A few days after coming home from the hospital, they discovered that their baby girl had a mass on her back. “I tried to get care for the baby, but everywhere we went, people asked if we had the health insurance card,” Mr. Sulaimon continues. “At Sacré-Cœur, the doctors sent us to Sainte-Justine, where we waited several hours in the emergency room.
On nous a dit que, sans carte, il fallai: They told us that without a card, we had to pay $721 to see a doctor. We couldn’t pay, so we went home without a doctor seeing my daughter. A pediatrician at Sacré-Cœur told me that if I didn’t get my child treated, I could be arrested for neglect; but without money, there was nothing I could do…” Fortunately, with the help of a social worker, the Sulaimons were able to set up a payment arrangement and get their daughter treated.
« On a finalement appris que la masse da: “We finally learned that the mass on her back wasn’t cancerous, but we had to talk to several specialists before even thinking about having it removed – which is expensive.” On top of the $9,000 bill owed to the Hôpital du Sacré-Cœur-de-Montréal, they currently owe nearly $13,000 to Sainte-Justine Hospital, Mr. Sulaimon tells us. Three months after his daughter’s birth, he received a letter confirming that because of her parents’ status, the little girl was not eligible for RAMQ, despite her Canadian citizenship. Through his social worker, Mr. Sulaimon was put in touch with the Montréal law firm Trudel Johnston & Lespérance. He is now the lead plaintiff in a class action against the Quebec government.
Me Marianne Dagenais-Lespérance, qui est: Lawyer Marianne Dagenais-Lespérance, who is involved in the class action, considers RAMQ’s practice a violation of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. She is seeking $5,000 in damages for each child who was denied access to care and $2,000 in additional compensation for each family, on top of reimbursement of costs. “This is a violation of the fundamental rights of children who are Canadian citizens and residents of Quebec,” she explains.
Sandra Escalera, résidente de Québec, mi: Sandra Escalera, a Quebec City resident, has been campaigning for children’s health care rights for several years. In 2014, while her husband was studying at Université Laval and she was going through the process of getting a work permit, their son Bruno, then five years old, was diagnosed with cancer. “Without access to RAMQ, you have to pay hundreds of dollars just to talk to a doctor,” she laments. “The first time I went to see the doctor with my son, he was crying in pain. I told them it was an emergency, and they asked me to pay. Afterward they saw just how urgent his situation was and they reimbursed me, but it was very stressful.”
Peu de temps après, Bruno a dû subir une: Shortly afterward, Bruno had to undergo an operation that required a stay in intensive care. When his insurance company stopped paying, Sandra turned to her friends and the local media. The family organized a crowdfunding campaign and several fundraisers to cover Bruno’s care. Some of his doctors also stopped billing the family. The child died in 2019, at the age of 10, shortly before his parents received their permanent residence.
« Je peux en parler aujourd’hui parce qu: “I can talk about it today because, despite everything, I’m very lucky,” says Ms. Escalera, now a CEGEP teacher. “We always managed to make it work, we never went into debt. I know a family whose daughter had leukemia, and they had to declare bankruptcy.”
Avec l’Association des parents-étudiants: Together with the Association des parents-étudiants de l’Université Laval, she is campaigning so that the children of international students and undocumented children can have access to health care. “Two years ago, it was decided that all children in Quebec had the right to go to school, regardless of their status,” she says. “If school is a right, why isn’t health care too?” she asks.

Rodrigue Barbe vit à Québec. Sa fille, E: Rodrigue Barbe lives in Quebec City. His five-year-old daughter, Elizabeth, was born at the Centre hospitalier de l’Université Laval (CHUL). He had access to RAMQ when their child was born, but his partner wasn’t eligible. Because the pregnancy was high-risk, the family now owes more than $97,000 to the CHUL. In 2014, Ms. Barbe had a miscarriage.
L’année suivante, quand elle a perdu ses: The following year, when her water broke at 24 weeks of pregnancy, the couple went to the Lévis hospital. The doctors quickly stabilized the mother before transferring her to the CHUL, where she stayed for 30 days.
« Elle avait une assurance privée avec u: “She had private insurance with a $10,000 limit,” Mr. Barbe recalls. “On the tenth day in the hospital, we learned we would be billed $3,300 a day.” On the day she was born, Elizabeth weighed barely a kilo. Two months in hospital were necessary. Mr. Barbe negotiated to have her care paid for by RAMQ, but despite all his efforts, he was unable to get the care given to his wife to save their daughter’s life covered.
« On a reçu des appels automatisés de l’: “We got automated calls from the hospital every day for two years,” Mr. Barbe recalls. “In the end, I blocked the number, but let’s be honest, our credit score is shit now.”
Barbe est un réfugié d’origine centrafri: Barbe is a refugee from the Central African Republic. He holds a doctorate but works in a restaurant while waiting to find a job in his field. His wife, who is originally from Cameroon, is a student and works part-time as a hairdresser. They look after Elizabeth, her little brother and her two teenage half-brothers. According to Mr. Barbe, their monstrous debt has taken a toll on their health and put pressure on their marriage.
« Je trouve tout ça difficile à comprend: “I find all of this hard to understand,” Mr. Barbe continues. “It’s unfair not to take care of a baby coming into the world or a pregnant woman. I know that sometimes the child isn’t eligible for RAMQ either. Why do they say they can’t take care of a child born in Quebec? When parents are neglectful, custody of the child can be taken away, but when the baby is still in its mother’s womb, they say the parents have to pay. That’s neglect too.”
Si le Québec est critiqué pour sa gestio: If Quebec is criticized for its handling of this issue, what are the other provinces doing? Ontario and British Columbia have given every child born on their territory access to health care for several decades. More recently, Nova Scotia (in 2015) and Alberta (in 2016) adopted the same approach, largely thanks to citizen engagement. Activists Syed Hussan and Marco Luciano were on the front lines of the fight that led to expanded access to health care in Alberta.
« Ça nous a pris plusieurs années avant: “It took us several years before we could bring the problem to the attention of our legislators,” explains Mr. Luciano, who is director of the migrant rights advocacy organization Migrante Alberta. “In 2013, an undocumented woman came to see us with her sick child and we realized she wasn’t eligible for health care. We did a lot of lobbying, we circulated a petition with 2,500 signatures and we managed to get the regulation changed. All in all, it went well, and now, all a mother has to do is show her child’s birth certificate for the baby to have access to care.”
Il ajoute que l’enjeu des droits des nou: He adds that the issue of newborns’ rights was a “winning” topic in Alberta. “The Conservatives had concerns about costs, but everyone knew it was shameful to debate the rights of little ones,” he says. Migrante Alberta also intends to ask the provincial government to give pregnant women access to prenatal care, regardless of their immigration status. “It’s important to make the connection between children’s rights and mothers’ right to health, and to immigration status,” Mr. Luciano stresses.
Tout le monde devrait avoir droit aux so: Everyone should have the right to health care, regardless of their status.” Syed Hussan, his colleague at the Toronto-based network Migrant Workers Alliance for Change, agrees. “We shouldn’t divide people into [immigration] categories and end up in a situation where the country’s 10 provinces and 3 territories have 13 different policies,” he says. “If the federal government granted permanent status to all these people, that would do it.”
Le ministre québécois de la Santé, Chris: Quebec Health Minister Christian Dubé said in July that he wanted to change certain practices so that children born in Canada to parents who aren’t eligible for RAMQ have access to health care. In an email to La Converse, RAMQ declined to comment further or provide a timeline in the wake of this announcement. This is neither the first time the Quebec government has been called on over this issue nor the first time a government has promised to act.
Me Dagenais-Lespérance rappelle que l’an: Dagenais-Lespérance points out that former premier Pauline Marois also promised to give these children access to RAMQ in 1999, when she was health minister in Lucien Bouchard’s government. Nothing changed, despite numerous reports, including from the Quebec Ombudsman’s office, the Observatoire des tout-petits and Médecins du Monde. “I feel like we’ve been fighting for this since the dawn of time,” exclaims psychiatrist Nicolas Bergeron, director of Médecins du Monde Canada (MDM). Since 2011, MDM has run a free clinic in downtown Montréal, where several families without status, awaiting status or otherwise ineligible for RAMQ get care for their children. The organization provides care to nearly 150 children a year, all of them Canadian citizens.
Le directeur du MDM – une organisation i: The director of MDM – an organization involved in the class action against the Quebec government – doesn’t want to declare victory following Minister Dubé’s announcement. “We have to see how [this statement] will be put into practice,” the psychiatrist says.
Selon lui, il faut « découpler le statut: In his view, Quebec needs to “decouple immigration status from access to health care.”
Il dénonce le fait que l’admissibilité d: He denounces the fact that a child’s eligibility for RAMQ depends on their parents’ status, which is not the case in other provinces. The doctor also fears that the minister’s statement doesn’t go far enough. “Why limit this announcement to babies when the parents have other minor children in their care?” he asks.
Mme Escalera abonde dans le même sens. E: Ms. Escalera agrees. She would like the health care system to be accessible to pregnant women, regardless of their status, so that their children avoid certain complications. “Without perinatal care, a baby risks being born with complications that the system will end up paying for,” she says. “It makes no sense.”
